label: rem:surreal-bounds-graded-mikusinski
title: Surreal-bound family as graded-Mikusiński std-collapse instances
html:
The four millennium-problem surreal bounds (Surreal bound for Birch--Swinnerton-Dyer: rank--order matches \omega-order of L-series, Surreal bound for the Riemann hypothesis: why \delta = 0 on the critical line, Surreal bound for P vs NP: Reeb-period transfinite exceeds classical-budget standard, Surreal bound for Collatz: contact-boundary deviation costs transfinite Reeb period) share a structural mechanism. The standard-part map \mathrm{std} \colon \mathbf{No} \to \mathbb{R} collapses a transfinite cost on the surreal-envelope side to a standard-real cost on the archimedean side, leaving a finite gap. Per Surreal squeeze: standard-scale cost dominates infinitesimal dissipation, the gap forces the inequality.

The graded-Mikusiński correspondence (GS-depth \leftrightarrow Goncharov period-depth correspondence) identifies these four remarks as the same construction at different depths of the iterated-integral filtration on \mathcal{H}_q:

Bound Conjecture interpreted Depth class Std-collapsed object
RH Collapse of the quantum gap \mathcal{P}_1 (logs) \zeta critical-line vanishing
BSD The q-deformed Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture \mathcal{P}_2 (regulators) L-function rank match
P vs NP P vs NP in the QOU: classical-limit separation of BQP-width classes \mathcal{P}_{\geq 1} (transfinite Reeb period) budget separation
Collatz The q-Collatz conjecture: Skein-module crossing resolution \mathcal{P}_2 (Bloch–Wigner shadow) contact-boundary deviation

The depth assignment above is conjectural modulo GS-depth \leftrightarrow Goncharov period-depth correspondence. The correspondence generates all four bounds via the single form:

\mathrm{std}\!\left( \text{depth-}n \text{ infinitesimal cost in } \mathbf{No} \right) > \text{standard archimedean budget},

where n ranges over the four classes and \mathrm{std} serves as the archimedean realization. The inequality direction is enforced by Surreal squeeze: standard-scale cost dominates infinitesimal dissipation.

Unifying the four bounds provides three concrete consequences. First, problem-specific squeezes are replaced with a universal std-collapse at a specified depth, analogous to Mikusiński's (1959) field of fractions unifying operational identities. Second, closing the squeeze at depth n for one millennium problem transports to any other problem at the same depth (e.g., depth-2 techniques for BSD \leftrightarrow Collatz). Third, the correspondence predicts a depth-3 surreal bound for any open problem whose archimedean reading involves weight-3 Goncharov periods (multiple zeta values \zeta(3), \zeta(2,1)), such as Apéry-style irrationality questions (Zagier 1986). For orientation on that programme: for every odd a \geq 3, \dim_{\mathbb{Q}} \mathrm{span}\{1, \zeta(3), \zeta(5), \ldots, \zeta(a)\} > 0.395 \log a [zudilin2001, Thm. 4]. This bounds a dimension; it does not decide the irrationality of any single \zeta(2k+1) with k \geq 2.

This relates to graded Titchmarsh. Mikusiński passes from C[0,\infty) to its field of fractions via Titchmarsh's no-zero-divisor theorem. The graded analog asks at which iterated-integral depth the *_q-product on \mathcal{H}_q first acquires zero divisors. Each surreal-bound remark is an obstruction to inverting a depth-n element, representing exactly the obstruction Mikusiński removes by passing to fractions. The four bounds are instances of graded Titchmarsh failure, each occurring at its characteristic depth.

The novel mathematical content resides in GS-depth \leftrightarrow Goncharov period-depth correspondence and its discharge targets.
